vsm1.6:1.1: Now, ten kinds of foulness, as corpses without consciousness, were listed next after the kasiṇas thus:
vsm1.6:1.2: the bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut up, the gnawed,
vsm1.6:1.3: the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the bleeding, the worm infested, a skeleton (III.105).
vsm1.6:1.4:
The bloated: it is bloated (uddhumāta) because bloated by gradual dilation and swelling
after (uddhaṃ) the close of life, as a bellows is with wind.
vsm1.6:1.5: What is bloated (uddhumāta) is the same as “the bloated” (uddhumātaka).
vsm1.6:1.6: Or alternatively, what is bloated (uddhumāta) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the bloated” (uddhumātaka).
vsm1.6:1.7: This is a term for a corpse in that particular state.
vsm1.6:2.1: The livid: what has patchy discolouration is called livid (vinīla).
vsm1.6:2.2: What is livid is the same as “the livid” (vinīlaka).
vsm1.6:2.3: Or alternatively, what is livid (vinīla) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the livid” (vinīlaka).
vsm1.6:2.4: This is a term for a corpse that is reddish-coloured in places where flesh is prominent,
vsm1.6:2.5: whitish-coloured in places where pus has collected,
vsm1.6:2.7: as if draped with blue-black cloth in the blue-black places.
vsm1.6:3.1: The festering: what is trickling with pus in broken places is festering (vipubba).
vsm1.6:3.2: What is festering is the same as “the festering” (vipubbaka).
vsm1.6:3.3: Or alternatively, what is festering (vipubba) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the festering” (vipubbaka).
vsm1.6:3.4: This is a term for a corpse in that particular state.
vsm1.6:4.1: The cut up: what has been opened up by cutting it in two is called cut up (vicchidda).
vsm1.6:4.2: What is cut up is the same as “the cut up” (vicchiddaka).
vsm1.6:4.3: Or alternatively, what is cut up (vicchidda) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the cut up” (vicchiddaka).
vsm1.6:4.4: This is a term for a corpse cut in the middle.
vsm1.6:5.1: The gnawed: what has been chewed here and there in various ways by dogs, jackals, etc., is what is gnawed (vikkhāyita).
vsm1.6:5.2: What is gnawed is the same as “the gnawed” (vikkhāyitaka).
vsm1.6:5.3: Or alternatively, what is gnawed (vikkhāyita) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness, thus it is “the gnawed” (vikkhāyitaka).
vsm1.6:5.4: This is a term for a corpse in that particular state.
vsm1.6:6.1: The scattered: what is strewed about (vividhaṃ khittaṃ) is scattered (vikkhittaṃ).
vsm1.6:6.2: What is scattered is the same as “the scattered” (vikkhittaka).
vsm1.6:6.3:
Or alternatively, what is scattered (vikkhitta) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness,
thus it is “the scattered” (vikkhittaka).
vsm1.6:6.4: This is a term for a corpse that is strewed here and there in this way: “Here a hand, there a foot, there the head” (cf. M I 58).
vsm1.6:7.1:
The hacked and scattered: it is hacked, and it is scattered in the way just described,
thus it is “hacked and scattered” (hata-vikkhittaka).
vsm1.6:7.2:
This is a term for a corpse scattered in the way just described after it
has been hacked with a knife in a crow’s-foot pattern on every limb.
vsm1.6:8.1: The bleeding: it sprinkles (kirati), scatters, blood (lohita), and it trickles here and there, thus it is “the bleeding” (lohitaka).
vsm1.6:8.2: This is a term for a corpse smeared with trickling blood.
vsm1.6:9.1:
The worm-infested: it is maggots that are called worms (puḷuva); it sprinkles worms
(puḷuve kirati), thus it is worm-infested (puḷuvaka).
vsm1.6:9.2: This is a term for a corpse full of maggots.
vsm1.6:10.1: A skeleton: bone (aṭṭhi) is the same as skeleton (aṭṭhika).
vsm1.6:10.2: Or alternatively, bone (aṭṭhi) is vile (kucchita) because of repulsiveness, thus it is a skeleton (aṭṭhika).
vsm1.6:10.3: This is a term both for a single bone and for a framework of bones.
vsm1.6:11.1: These names are also used both for the signs that arise with the bloated, etc., as their support,
vsm1.6:11.2: and for the jhānas obtained in the signs.
vsm1.6:12.1: Herein, when a meditator wants to develop the jhāna called “of the bloated” by arousing the sign of the bloated on a bloated body,
vsm1.6:12.2: he should in the way already described approach a teacher of the kind mentioned under the earth kasiṇa
vsm1.6:12.3: and learn the meditation subject from him.
vsm1.6:12.4: In explaining the meditation subject to him, the teacher should explain it all, that is,
vsm1.6:12.5: the directions for going with the aim of acquiring the sign of foulness,
vsm1.6:12.6: the characterizing of the surrounding signs,
vsm1.6:12.7: the eleven ways of apprehending the sign,
vsm1.6:12.8: the reviewing of the path gone by and come by,
vsm1.6:12.9: concluding with the directions for absorption.
vsm1.6:12.10: And when the meditator has learnt it all well,
vsm1.6:12.11: he should go to an abode of the kind already described
vsm1.6:12.12: and live there while seeking the sign of the bloated.
vsm1.6:13.1: Meanwhile, when he hears people saying that at some village gate or on some road or at some forest’s edge or
vsm1.6:13.2: at the base of some rock or at the root of some tree or on some charnel ground a bloated corpse is lying,
vsm1.6:13.3: he should not go there at once, like one who plunges into a river where there is no ford.
vsm1.6:14.2: Because this foulness is beset by wild beasts and non-human beings,
vsm1.6:14.3: and he might risk his life there.
vsm1.6:14.4: Or perhaps the way to it goes by a village gate or a bathing place or an irrigated field,
vsm1.6:14.5: and there a visible object of the opposite sex might come into focus.
vsm1.6:14.6: Or perhaps the body is of the opposite sex;
vsm1.6:14.7: for a female body is unsuitable for a man, and a male body for a woman.
vsm1.6:14.8: If only recently dead, it may even look beautiful;
vsm1.6:14.9: hence there might be danger to the life of purity.
vsm1.6:14.10: But if he judges himself thus, “This is not difficult for one like me,” then he can go there.
vsm1.6:15.1: And when he goes, he should do so only after he has spoken to the senior elder of the Community or to some well-known bhikkhu.
vsm1.6:16.2:
Because if all his limbs are seized with shuddering at the charnel ground, or if his gorge rises when he
is confronted with disagreeable objects such as the visible forms and sounds of non-human beings, lions, tigers, etc.,
vsm1.6:16.4: then he whom he told will have his bowl and robe well looked after in the monastery,
vsm1.6:16.5: or he will care for him by sending young bhikkhus or novices to him.
vsm1.6:17.1: Besides, robbers may meet there thinking a charnel ground a safe place for them whether or not they have done anything wrong.
vsm1.6:17.2: And when men chase them, they drop their goods near the bhikkhu and run away.
vsm1.6:17.3: Perhaps the men seize the bhikkhu, saying “We have found the thief with the goods,” and bully him.
vsm1.6:17.4: Then he whom he told will explain to the men “Do not bully him; he went to do this special work after telling me,”
vsm1.6:17.6: This is the advantage of going only after informing someone.
vsm1.6:18.1: Therefore he should inform a bhikkhu of the kind described
vsm1.6:18.2: and then set out eager to see the sign,
vsm1.6:18.3: and as happy and joyful as a warrior-noble (khattiya) on his way to the scene of anointing,
vsm1.6:18.4: as one going to offer libations at the hall of sacrifice,
vsm1.6:18.5: or as a pauper on his way to unearth a hidden treasure.
vsm1.6:18.6: And he should go there in the way advised by the Commentaries.
vsm1.6:19.2: “One who is learning the bloated sign of foulness
vsm1.6:19.5: with his sense faculties turned inwards,
vsm1.6:19.6: with his mind not turned outwards,
vsm1.6:19.7: reviewing the path gone by and come by.
vsm1.6:19.8: In the place where the bloated sign of foulness has been left
vsm1.6:19.9: he notes any stone or termite-mound or tree or bush or creeper there each with its particular sign
vsm1.6:19.10: and in relation to the object.
vsm1.6:19.12: he characterizes the bloated sign of foulness by the fact of its having attained that particular individual essence. (see §84)
vsm1.6:19.13:
Then he sees that the sign is properly apprehended, that it is properly remembered, that it is properly
defined, by its colour, by its mark, by its shape, by its direction, by its location, by its delimitation,
by its joints, by its openings, by its concavities, by its convexities, and all round.
vsm1.6:20.1: “When he has properly apprehended the sign, properly remembered it, properly defined it,
vsm1.6:20.2: he goes alone with no companion,
vsm1.6:20.4: with his sense faculties turned inwards,
vsm1.6:20.5: with his mind not turned outwards,
vsm1.6:20.6: reviewing the path gone by and come by.
vsm1.6:20.7: When he walks, he resolves that his walk is oriented towards it;
vsm1.6:20.8: when he sits, he prepares a seat that is oriented towards it.
vsm1.6:21.1: “What is the purpose, what is the advantage of characterizing the surrounding signs?
vsm1.6:21.2: Characterizing the surrounding signs has non-delusion for its purpose, it has non-delusion for its advantage.
vsm1.6:21.3: What is the purpose, what is the advantage of apprehending the sign in the other eleven ways?
vsm1.6:21.4: Apprehending the sign in the other eleven ways has anchoring the mind for its purpose, it has anchoring the mind for its advantage.
vsm1.6:21.5: What is the purpose, what is the advantage of reviewing the path gone by and come by?
vsm1.6:21.6:
Reviewing the path gone by and come by has keeping the mind on the track for its purpose,
it has keeping the mind on the track for its advantage.
vsm1.6:22.1: “When he has established reverence for it by seeing its advantages and by perceiving it as a treasure and so come to love it,
vsm1.6:22.2: he anchors his mind upon that object:
vsm1.6:22.3: ‘Surely in this way I shall be liberated from ageing and death.’
vsm1.6:22.4: Quite secluded from sense desires, secluded from unprofitable things he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna … seclusion.
vsm1.6:22.5: He has arrived at the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere.
vsm1.6:22.6: His is a heavenly abiding and an instance of the meritorious action consisting in meditative development.” (Source untraced.)
vsm1.6:23.1: So if he goes to the charnel ground to test his control of mind, let him do so after striking the gong or summoning a chapter.
vsm1.6:23.2: If he goes there mainly for developing that meditation subject,
vsm1.6:23.3: let him go alone with no companion,
vsm1.6:23.4: without renouncing his basic meditation subject and keeping it always in mind,
vsm1.6:23.5: taking a walking stick or a staff to keep off attacks by dogs, etc.,
vsm1.6:23.6: ensuring unremitting mindfulness by establishing it well,
vsm1.6:23.7: with his mind not turned outwards because he has ensured that his faculties, of which his mind is the sixth, are turned inwards.
vsm1.6:24.1: As he goes out of the monastery he should note the gate: “I have gone out in such a direction by such a gate.”
vsm1.6:24.2: After that he should define the path by which he goes:
vsm1.6:24.3: “This path goes in an easterly direction … westerly … northerly … southerly direction”
vsm1.6:24.4: or “It goes in an intermediate direction”;
vsm1.6:24.5: and “In this place it goes to the left, in this place to the right”;
vsm1.6:24.6: and “In this place there is a stone, in this a termite-mound, in this a tree, in this a bush, in this a creeper.”
vsm1.6:24.7: He should go to the place where the sign is, defining in this way the path by which he goes.
vsm1.6:25.1: And he should not approach it upwind;
vsm1.6:25.2: for if he did so and the smell of corpses assailed his nose,
vsm1.6:25.4: or he might throw up his food,
vsm1.6:25.5: or he might repent his coming, thinking “What a place of corpses I have come to!”
vsm1.6:25.6: So instead of approaching it upwind, he should go downwind.
vsm1.6:25.7: If he cannot go by a downwind path—
vsm1.6:25.8: if there is a mountain or a ravine or a rock or a fence or a patch of thorns or water or a bog in the way—
vsm1.6:25.9: then he should go stopping his nose with the corner of his robe.
vsm1.6:25.10: These are the duties in going.
vsm1.6:26.1: When he has gone there in this way, he should not at once look at the sign of foulness;
vsm1.6:26.2: he should make sure of the direction.
vsm1.6:26.3: For perhaps if he stands in a certain direction, the object does not appear clearly to him and his mind is not wieldy.
vsm1.6:26.4: So rather than there he should stand where the object appears clearly and his mind is wieldy.
vsm1.6:26.5: And he should avoid standing to leeward or to windward of it.
vsm1.6:26.6: For if he stands to leeward he is bothered by the corpse smell and his mind strays;
vsm1.6:26.7: and if he stands to windward and non-human beings are dwelling there, they may get annoyed and do him a mischief.
vsm1.6:26.8: So he should move round a little and not stand too much to windward.
vsm1.6:27.1: Then he should stand not too far off or too near, or too much towards the feet or the head.
vsm1.6:27.2: For if he stands too far off, the object is not clear to him,
vsm1.6:27.3: and if he stands too near, he may get frightened.
vsm1.6:27.4: If he stands too much towards the feet or the head, not all the foulness becomes manifest to him equally.
vsm1.6:27.5: So he should stand not too far off or too near, opposite the middle of the body, in a place convenient for him to look at it.
vsm1.6:28.1:
Then he should characterize the surrounding signs in the way stated thus: “In the place where the bloated
sign of foulness has been left he notes any stone … or creeper there with its sign” (§19).
vsm1.6:29.1: These are the directions for characterizing them.
vsm1.6:29.2: If there is a rock in the eye’s focus near the sign,
vsm1.6:29.3: he should define it in this way: “This rock is high or low, small or large, brown or black or white, long or round,”
vsm1.6:29.4: after which he should observe the relative positions thus: “In this place, this is a rock, this is the sign of foulness;
vsm1.6:29.5: this is the sign of foulness, this is a rock.”
vsm1.6:30.2: he should define it in this way: “This is high or low, small or large, brown or black or white, long or round,”
vsm1.6:30.3: after which he should observe the relative positions thus: “In this place, this is a termite-mound, this is the sign of foulness.”
vsm1.6:31.2: he should define it in this way: “This is a pipal fig tree or a banyan fig tree or a kacchaka fig tree or a kapittha fig tree;
vsm1.6:31.3: it is tall or short, small or large, black or white,”
vsm1.6:31.4: after which he should observe the relative positions thus: “In this place, this is a tree, this is the sign of foulness.”
vsm1.6:32.2: he should define it in this way: “This is a sindi bush or a karamanda bush or a kaṇavīra bush or a koraṇḍaka bush;
vsm1.6:32.3: it is tall or short, small or large,”
vsm1.6:32.4: after which he should observe the relative positions thus: “In this place, this is a bush, this is the sign of foulness.”
vsm1.6:33.2:
he should define it in this way: “This is a pumpkin creeper or a gourd creeper or a brown
creeper or a black creeper or a stinking creeper,”
vsm1.6:33.3: after which he should observe the relative positions thus: “In this place, this is a creeper, this is the sign of foulness;
vsm1.6:33.4: this is the sign of foulness, this is a creeper.”
vsm1.6:34.1: Also with its particular sign and in relation to the object was said (§19); but that is included by what has just been said;
vsm1.6:34.2: for he “characterizes it with its particular sign” when he defines it again and again,
vsm1.6:34.3:
and he “characterizes it in relation to the object” when he defines it by combining it each
time in pairs thus: “This is a rock, this is the sign of foulness;
vsm1.6:34.4: this is the sign of foulness, this is a rock.”
vsm1.6:35.2:
again he should bring to mind the fact that it has an individual essence, its own state of being bloated, which is not common
to anything else, since it was said that he defines it by the fact of its having attained that particular individual essence.
vsm1.6:35.3:
The meaning is that it should be defined according to individual essence,
according to its own nature, as “the inflated, the bloated.”
vsm1.6:35.4: Having defined it in this way,
vsm1.6:35.5: he should apprehend the sign in the following six ways, that is to say, (1) by its colour, (2) by its mark, (3) by its shape,
vsm1.6:35.6: (4) by its direction, (5) by its location, (6) by its delimitation.
vsm1.6:36.1: (1) The meditator should define it by its colour thus: “This is the body of one who is black or white or yellow-skinned.”
vsm1.6:37.1: (2) Instead of defining it by the female mark or the male mark, he should define it by its mark thus:
vsm1.6:37.2: “This is the body of one who was in the first phase of life, in the middle phase, in the last phase.”
vsm1.6:38.1: (3) By its shape: he should define it only by the shape of the bloated thus:
vsm1.6:38.2: “This is the shape of its head, this is the shape of its neck, this is the shape of its hand,
vsm1.6:38.3: this is the shape of its chest, this is the shape of its belly, this is the shape of its navel,
vsm1.6:38.4: this is the shape of its hips, this is the shape of its thigh, this is the shape of its calf, this is the shape of its foot.”
